62d6101520:
This chapter shows how an agent is actually built. We write the loop and its harness from nothing on the raw Messages API. That means the request, the stop_reason that steers it, and the tool_use and tool_result blocks that carry work back and forth. It also means the budgets that stop a runaway, and the error path.

Then we look at what the Claude Agent SDK packages for you. We see where Anthropic-hosted Managed Agents move the loop off your machines entirely. And we see how hooks turn "please always do X" into code that runs every time.
01974cdaaf: Where the neighbours are: chapter 01 decides whether you need an agent, and how agents are arranged (workflow patterns, orchestrator and subagents). Chapter 03 covers memory, context management and third-party frameworks. Chapter 20 covers hooks as a security control (blocking destructive actions, secrets). This chapter is the construction layer between them.
f0dd506489:
An agent is a loop you own: send the whole conversation to the model, read stop_reason, and while it says "tool_use" run the requested tools and send back one user message of tool_result blocks with matching ids; stop when it says "end_turn" (or a budget runs out, which you report as a failure, not a success).

The Claude Agent SDK is that loop already written, with built-in tools, permissions, sessions and hooks, running in your process; Anthropic-hosted Managed Agents run the same kind of loop and its sandbox on Anthropic's infrastructure, and hooks are the place you put anything that must happen deterministically rather than when the model remembers.
aa7b1352ea:
Every question the exam asks about objective 1.2 is one of those clauses wearing a scenario:

  • "The agent stopped after the first tool call" is a loop that checked the text instead of stop_reason.
  • "The API returns 400 after a parallel tool call" is a history where results were split or an id was lost.
  • "The formatter only runs most of the time" is a rule written in a prompt that should have been a PostToolUse hook.
  • "We need hours-long runs and have two engineers" points towards a hosted harness.
  • "The tools must reach an on-premise inventory system and data cannot leave our tenancy" points back to self-hosting.
a305c0f1db:
A Spring analogy runs through the chapter. The harness is a saga orchestrator:

  • each model response is an event, and stop_reason is its type;
  • the tool dispatcher is the set of participants;
  • the message list is the saga log;
  • hooks are the interceptors (a HandlerInterceptor or an AOP @Around advice) that run on every call, whether or not the business code remembers them.

You've built all of these before. Only the participant that chooses the next step is new.
bc2a1fe6a9: The word harness comes from test engineering. It's the scaffolding that drives a unit under test, feeds it inputs and records outputs. In agent work it means the same thing. The model is the unit, and all it can do is map a list of messages to one more message. Everything that makes it act, remember, stop, or be safe is the harness around it.
5a7b677ed9:
The first agents were prompts. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) asked the model to write Thought, Action and Observation lines. A Python script scanned the output with regular expressions, ran the action, and pasted the observation back. It stopped when it saw Finish[...]. The harness was a parser plus a while loop.

It broke whenever the model formatted an action slightly differently, or wrote the word "Finish" in the middle of a thought. Both the action and the termination signal were free text.
a22801b64b:
Model providers then moved tool calling into the API. You declare tools as JSON Schema. The model returns a typed tool_use block with an id, a name and an input object. And the response carries an explicit stop_reason that says why generation ended. The harness stopped being a parser and became a dispatcher.

This is the protocol you still use, and the one the exam tests. Structured signals replaced the textual ones. Every anti-pattern in section 07 is a way of going back to reading text.
3469ef3231:
Once everyone was writing the same loop, the loop got packaged. Anthropic's SDKs gained a tool runner helper that runs the loop for local functions.

Claude Code (2025) is a harness for software work: file and shell tools, permissions, hooks, context compaction, subagents. Its engine was released as a library, first called the Claude Code SDK. In late 2025 it was renamed the Claude Agent SDK, since people use it for agents that have nothing to do with code.

In 2026 Anthropic added Claude Managed Agents, a hosted harness. You define an agent and an environment, start a session, and exchange events with a loop that runs, with its sandbox, on Anthropic's side.

The protocol at the bottom never changed. Each layer moved more of the harness out of your code.
723ec69dd1: Strip any agent framework down and you find the same five responsibilities. Naming them gives you a checklist for reviewing someone else's agent. It also maps what each packaged option takes off your hands.
e72e5c059e: Carry the conversation. The model is stateless. The harness owns messages[]. It appends every assistant turn exactly as returned, and every tool result turn, and it resends the whole list each call. Persisting that list is what makes resume possible.
e2d01cf63e: Dispatch tools. Look up the tool by name, validate input, and run it. Turn exceptions into is_error results. Return results in one user turn with the right ids.
9883b5c66c: Enforce limits and policy. Turn caps, token or dollar budgets, wall-clock timeouts, permission checks, approval gates, and hooks. These are the parts the model can't be trusted to do for itself.
3595a84a48: Notice what's not on the list: deciding which tool to call, in which order, or when the task is finished. Those are the model's decisions in an agent. If your harness makes them (a fixed sequence of calls, or a classifier up front that chooses one path), you've built a workflow. That may be the right answer, and chapter 01 is where you make that choice. The harness constrains the model's choices. It doesn't replace them.
b480a0939e: Before writing the loop, look at exactly what crosses the network. A request carries a model id, max_tokens, an optional system string, the tools array (name, description, JSON Schema), and messages. The response is one assistant message: a content array of blocks, a stop_reason, and usage. Companion example 01_wire_anatomy.py prints one:
1530912dfb:
Three facts in that output carry the whole chapter.

  • The model didn't execute anything. A tool_use block is a request addressed to your code.
  • The block has an id that you must echo back, so the API can tie the result to the request.
  • stop_reason is "tool_use". That's the API telling you, in a typed field, that the turn ended because the model is waiting for tool output. It hasn't finished.
4c7c3000a5: The next request must contain three messages. First, the original user message. Second, this assistant message unchanged: both blocks, including the text and, when thinking is enabled, any thinking blocks with their signatures. Third, a new user message whose content begins with a tool_result block for toolu_01A. That three-message shape is the minimum valid history after a tool call.
0bfe7dca86:
The API enforces only a few rules on that history, and they're strict.

  • Roles alternate, starting from user. The API tolerates consecutive same-role turns in some cases by merging them, but a harness should never rely on that.
  • Every tool_use in an assistant message must have a matching tool_result in the immediately following user message.
  • Tool result blocks go first in that user message. Any text you want to add comes after them.

The companion fake_client.py enforces these rules locally. A broken loop fails in your terminal, the way it would fail against the API, instead of passing silently.
46004a8d36: Here is the smallest loop that is correct. Type it out once from memory. Every packaged harness is this code plus features, and exam distractors are almost always this code with one line changed.
87c60d7305:
Read the six numbered comments as six exam answers.

  • (1) The assistant turn is appended with all its blocks, as the API returned them. Filtering it to "just the text" orphans the tool ids.
  • (2) stop_reason is the only signal that decides whether to continue. The text is for humans.
  • (3) A single response can contain several tool_use blocks, and the model expects all of them answered.
  • (4) A failing tool becomes an is_error result that the model can read and react to. The loop doesn't crash, and it doesn't pretend the call succeeded.
  • (5) All results go back in one user message.
  • (6) Running out of turns is reported as an error. A caller that receives a return value can assume the agent finished. One that receives an exception knows it didn't.
9cc5e9558a: The trace from the companion run is four messages long. That's the shape of every successful single-tool run:
3971978856:
Sometimes your tools are plain local functions and you don't need per-step control. For that case, the Python and TypeScript SDKs offer a beta tool runner. It generates schemas from typed functions and runs exactly this loop.

It's a convenience, not a different design. It still branches on stop_reason, still turns exceptions into error results, and still takes an iteration cap as a safety budget. Check the SDK docs for the current helper names (in Python at the time of writing, a @beta_tool decorator and client.beta.messages.tool_runner(...)).
3aa9bddd7a:
Use the runner for scripts and prototypes. Write the loop yourself when you need something between the model's request and the tool's execution: an approval step, a persistence checkpoint, concurrency rules for tools with side effects, or a trace span per call.

That "something in between" is the reason harnesses exist. It's also why the exam treats a hand-written loop as a design skill rather than boilerplate.
4d3f313fea:
A response can end for several reasons, and each needs a different action. The common bug is a two-way branch (if tool_use ... else done) that treats a truncated answer or a refusal as a finished one.

The robust shape is an explicit switch with a default that fails loudly. Then, if a future release adds a value to the API, it shows up as an error in your logs, not as a silently wrong answer.
43520a33ad:
Two of these deserve a closer look, because tested scenarios hide there.

A max_tokens stop inside a tool call is easy to mistake for a tool call. The response contains a tool_use block, but its input JSON was cut off, and stop_reason says max_tokens, not tool_use. A harness that inspects blocks rather than the stop reason will try to run a tool with half its arguments.

And pause_turn is a continue signal that does not involve your tools at all. The server-side tool loop needs another request to keep going. So you resend the conversation without adding a tool result.
69ed3cbadc:
Claude can request several independent tools in one turn. For example: look up the order, and check for an outage at the customer's ZIP code. Each request has its own id.

The harness may run them concurrently, since the model declared them independent by requesting them together. But it must return every result in a single user message. Splitting them into one user message per result produces a history the API documentation explicitly warns against. It also teaches the model to stop making parallel calls. A strict validator, like the companion's, rejects it outright:
6f4af5cdf0:
Should parallel calls run concurrently in your process? For reads, yes. That's the latency win the model offered you. For tools with side effects, decide per tool. Two issue_credit calls for the same account in one turn may be a duplicate the model didn't notice.

A production dispatcher keeps a small table of which tools are safe to run concurrently, and serialises the rest. It also makes side-effecting tools idempotent, with a key derived from the tool_use id, so a retried turn doesn't double-charge.
fdabd9c34d: When a tool fails, the model needs to know, in words it can act on. Return a tool_result with is_error: true and a message that says what was wrong and what would be right. The companion's lookup rejects a bare account number. The model reads the error and retries with the right format. It all happens inside the loop, with no human involved:
3f478cd27b:
The two wrong alternatives are both common. Raising the exception out of the loop kills the whole run, over something the model could have fixed. Returning an empty or success-shaped result ("[]", "ok") makes the model believe the call worked, and it reasons from a false fact.

Chapter 12 (debugging) goes into retryable versus non-retryable errors and structured error payloads. Here the rule is simple: an error is information for the model, flagged as an error.
af3b9ebcba: Companion 07_broken_loops.py runs one scripted conversation through three broken loops and one fixed one. The model's first message says "I'm done checking the first system. Now the second." It also requests a tool. That one sentence is enough to break two of them.
c8827a621d:
Because the API is stateless, every call resends everything: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the entire history. So input tokens grow with each turn, and the total cost of a run grows roughly with the square of its length.

Take a ten-turn run with 2,000 tokens of tool output per turn. It doesn't cost ten times a one-turn run. It costs closer to fifty times, because turn ten pays for turns one to nine again.

Prompt caching (chapter 13 and the caching sections of chapter 18) recovers much of this for the stable prefix. Context management (chapter 03) trims the growing tail. But the harness still needs budgets.
aed79a9254: A good harness has more than one limit, and each one exists for a different failure:
202e54a7e1: The point of the subtype is honesty. When a budget fires, the caller must be able to tell "the agent finished" from "we stopped it". The Agent SDK's result message does exactly this: subtype is "success" or one of the error values, and is_error is set. Your own harness should do the same. Otherwise a dashboard counting successes quietly counts budget exhaustion as success.
9a8b81821a: The companion's harness.py grows the loop into something you could put behind an API. It has a tool registry, hooks keyed by event with a tool-name matcher, an approval callback, budgets, and a result object with a subtype. It's deliberately shaped like the Agent SDK's surface. So when you read the SDK docs in section 10, every option maps to something you've already seen work.
3b0b953149:
Three design choices in it are worth defending in a review.

  • The policy check sits inside the dispatcher, between the model's request and the tool's execution. No code path can run a tool without passing through it.
  • A denial goes back to the model as an error result with a reason. It isn't swallowed. The model can then choose a different approach (example 09 shows it switching from kubectl delete to kubectl get).
  • The Stop hook can send the agent back to work, so completion itself is gated. That's how you guarantee "tests pass before the agent says done" without trusting the model to check.
965f6cb825:
The Claude Agent SDK is the harness behind Claude Code, published as a library for Python (pip install claude-agent-sdk) and TypeScript (@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk). Section 09 wrote a harness. The SDK gives you a finished one:

  • the loop;
  • built-in tools for files, shell, search and the web (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep, WebSearch, WebFetch and others);
  • a permission system;
  • hooks;
  • sessions you can resume and fork;
  • subagents;
  • MCP client support;
  • automatic context compaction.

It runs in your process and on your infrastructure. That's what makes it the "self-hosted" option in section 14. (Under the hood, the Python package drives a bundled Claude Code runtime. In current versions you don't need to install the CLI separately, but check the docs for your version.)
f5904204a8:
query(prompt=..., options=...) is an async iterator for a one-shot task. It starts a session, runs the agent until it finishes or hits a limit, and yields every message along the way.

ClaudeSDKClient is an async context manager that keeps a session open. You can send follow-up prompts, interrupt a running turn, and register custom tools and hooks that live for the conversation.

Rule of thumb: a batch job or CI step uses query(). A chat-style app, or anything with a human in the loop, uses the client.
18a631a635:
Custom tools reach the SDK as MCP tools. The @tool decorator plus create_sdk_mcp_server builds an in-process MCP server, with no subprocess and no network. Its tools are named mcp__<server key>__<tool>. That's the name you put in allowed_tools and in hook matchers.

External MCP servers (stdio or HTTP) go in the same mcp_servers map. Chapter 22 covers MCP servers in depth. The point here is that the SDK has one tool interface, MCP, for everything that isn't built in.
5aacf3ccfe: ClaudeAgentOptions has around fifty fields. These are the ones scenarios turn on. All names below were checked against the Python SDK reference. TypeScript uses camelCase equivalents (allowedTools, permissionMode, maxTurns, settingSources).
c5015cd246:
One permission detail is easy to get wrong, and the SDK reference spells it out. can_use_tool runs only when the permission flow would otherwise prompt. A call already approved by allowed_tools, an allow rule, or the permission mode never reaches it. If you need to see every tool call (to log it, count it, or block it), use a PreToolUse hook, which runs first.

The next figure shows the order in which the SDK evaluates a tool call. Treat the exact order of the middle steps as "check the docs". The two ends are stable: hooks first, the callback last.
7d5f5fcf5d:
The SDK yields typed messages:

  • a SystemMessage at start (subtype init, with the session id and tool list);
  • AssistantMessages holding text and tool-use blocks;
  • UserMessages holding tool results;
  • finally, a ResultMessage.

The result message is the one your code acts on. Its fields include subtype ("success", "error_max_turns", "error_max_budget_usd", "error_during_execution", "error_max_structured_output_retries"), is_error, result (the final text), num_turns, total_cost_usd, usage and session_id. Companion example 13 emulates this stream, so you can practise the consumer side offline:
f958d19a78: The stream is the conversation from section 05, typed. Take that mental model into the exam. The SDK doesn't have a different protocol. It has your loop with the plumbing done, and it hands you the history as it goes.
7660c554b6:
The SDK is Claude Code's engine, so it can load the same filesystem configuration: CLAUDE.md memory, .claude/settings.json (permissions and shell hooks), skills, slash commands and agent definitions. setting_sources controls which of these load.

Behaviour here has changed across versions. An early release loaded nothing by default; current docs describe the default query() options as including settings sources. So for a production service, set setting_sources explicitly. Use [] for a hermetic agent whose behaviour is defined entirely in code. Use ["project"] when the repository's CLAUDE.md and hooks should apply.

An agent whose behaviour changes because someone edited a file in the working directory is a debugging story waiting to happen.
d011ede648:
A session is a persisted conversation with an id. Every SDK run has one; it's in the init system message and the result message.

  • Passing resume=<session_id> continues it with full history.
  • continue_conversation=True continues the most recent one in the working directory.
  • Adding fork_session=True to a resume creates a new session that starts from the old history, leaving the original untouched.

Claude Code exposes the same ideas as claude --resume / --continue and --fork-session.
fb0be6d428: In your own harness, the same capability is just persistence of messages[]. Example 14 writes the history as JSON after every turn and reloads it in a "new process". It forks it by copying under a new id:
b1756b05db: When not to resume: when the world changed since the session ran. Maybe files were edited, tickets closed, or prices moved. The old tool results in the history are now stale facts, and the model will trust them. Starting a fresh session with a short written summary of what was decided is often more reliable than resuming a long session full of outdated observations. Chapter 03 returns to this under context management.
73cf94fbc2:
Here is the core distinction of the second half of the objective. A system prompt instruction such as "always run the formatter after editing a file" is followed most of the time. Most isn't always. Over a long session, with a full context and competing instructions, the model will sometimes skip it.

Some requirements must have a failure rate of zero: compliance logging, formatting, a test gate, redaction, a hard block. They can't live in the prompt. They have to live in code that the harness runs at a fixed point in the lifecycle, every time, regardless of what the model decides. That code is a hook.
6dbc3c189a: The Java parallel is exact. You'd never implement "every controller call must be audited" by adding a comment asking each developer to log. You'd write a HandlerInterceptor or an @Around aspect. Prompts are the comment. Hooks are the interceptor.
86aa882c25:
An SDK hook is an async function (input_data, tool_use_id, context) -> dict, registered under an event name with an optional matcher. For tool events, the matcher is tested against the tool name. It can be an exact name ("Bash"), a pipe list ("Write|Edit"), or a regular expression ("^mcp__").

Matchers see only the tool name, never its arguments. So filtering by file path or command content happens inside the hook. Every input carries session_id, cwd and hook_event_name. Tool events add tool_name and tool_input, and PostToolUse adds the tool's response.
79e713cfcb:
The return value has two layers.

Top-level fields apply to any event. systemMessage is shown to the user, not the model. continue (spelled continue_ in Python) stops the agent.

hookSpecificOutput controls the current operation. For PreToolUse, that's permissionDecision ("allow", "deny", "ask", "defer"), permissionDecisionReason (fed back to the model so it doesn't retry blindly) and updatedInput. For PostToolUse, it's additionalContext (appended to the result) or updatedToolOutput (replaces it).

Returning {} means "no opinion, carry on". When several hooks match, they run in parallel and the most restrictive decision wins. One deny blocks the call, whatever the others say.
ebfae0ff9d:
Companion examples 09 to 11 run the three most tested shapes against the harness.

  • In example 09, a careless "approve everything" hook and a strict "block destructive commands" hook both match. Deny wins. The model reads the reason and chooses a read-only command instead.
  • In example 10, a PostToolUse hook turns a legacy pipe-delimited CRM record and a modern JSON record into the same JSON shape. It also redacts a Social Security number before the model ever sees it.

In example 11, a Stop hook refuses to let the agent finish while a test is failing:
7dadbd6f53:
The prompt isn't useless after the fix. It still tells the model the policy, so the model plans sensibly (offer $50 and escalate the rest, as example 12 shows). The difference is that the prompt now shapes behaviour, and the hook guarantees it.

The exam phrases to look for are "must", "always", "every time", "guarantee", "compliance" and "audit". Each one points away from prompt wording and towards a hook.
35961a1801:
Claude Code and the SDK (when setting_sources loads them) also accept hooks defined as shell commands in settings.json. The event names and the JSON output format are the same as SDK callbacks. The transport is different. The hook process receives the event as JSON on stdin, and answers with an exit code and optional JSON on stdout.

  • Exit code 0 means success; stdout JSON is parsed for decisions.
  • Exit code 2 is a blocking error, and its stderr is fed back to Claude.
  • Other non-zero codes are non-blocking errors.

Check the hooks reference for the exact per-event behaviour of exit code 2.
a1c714e379:
Note the stop_hook_active check. A Stop hook that always blocks makes an agent that can never finish. The flag tells the hook that the agent is already continuing because of a previous block. So a well-written hook lets it stop the second time, or after a counter.

That's the hook-level version of the budget rule from section 08: every mechanism that can extend a loop needs its own limit.
054b5e91ca:
Which form should you use? In an SDK application, use callbacks. They're typed, testable with your unit tests, and can share state with the rest of your service. In a repository that people work in with Claude Code, use settings-file hooks. They're versioned with the code, and they apply to every developer and to claude -p in CI.

The configuration side (settings scopes, precedence, managed settings) is chapter 10. The security use of the same mechanism is chapter 20.
4d120388f1:
Every agent has three moving parts:

  • the loop: the code that calls the model and dispatches tools;
  • the tool execution environment: where shell commands run and files live;
  • the state: the conversation history, files produced, session records.

"Self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted" is the question of where those three parts run, and who operates them.
e8c73ab3d6:
Self-hosted means the loop runs in your process: your own Messages API loop, the SDK tool runner, or the Claude Agent SDK. The model call goes to Anthropic (or to Claude on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI or Microsoft Foundry). But tools execute on your machines, inside your network, with your credentials. The history lives where you store it.

You get full control of tools, network reach, data handling and per-step policy. You also own the containers, scaling, sandboxing of shell access, session storage, retries and upgrades.
9778d20159:
Anthropic-hosted means Claude Managed Agents: a configurable harness that runs on Anthropic's infrastructure. You define two things:

  • an agent: model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers, skills;
  • an environment: where sessions run. That's either an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox with packages and controlled network access, or a self-hosted sandbox on your infrastructure.

Then you start sessions. Your application exchanges events with a running session over server-sent events.

The platform runs the loop, the built-in tools (bash, file operations, web search and fetch, MCP), prompt caching and compaction for you. It stores the event history server-side. So a session can run for minutes or hours, be steered with further messages, or be interrupted.
f4719f168a:
Constraints drive the decision, not taste. Companion example 16 turns it into a function you can argue with.

Hard constraints come first. A requirement for zero data retention or a HIPAA BAA rules out the hosted option as documented today. Tools that must run behind your firewall favour self-hosting (or a self-hosted sandbox). Maybe you need an approval gate, a custom persistence step, or detailed telemetry between every model request and tool execution. That favours your own loop.

Then the soft constraints. A small team that needs long-running, asynchronous agents with a sandbox, and doesn't want to operate one, leans hosted. An application that wants Claude Code's tool set embedded in its own service leans Agent SDK.
ae6a52146d:
The hosted model has four nouns, and the documentation uses them consistently.

  • An agent is the reusable definition: model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills. You create it once and reference it by id.
  • An environment is where sessions run. An example is an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox with a networking policy that allows package managers.
  • A session is one running instance of an agent in an environment, doing one task.
  • Events are what flows between your application and the session. You send user turns, plus tool results for any custom tools you execute yourself. The session streams back agent messages, tool-use notices and status changes.
9007326feb:
Compare this with section 05. There's no stop_reason switch, no dispatcher and no history list in your code. The hosted harness runs that loop. Your code is an event consumer, and session.status_idle plays the role that end_turn played for you before. The agent definition's toolset replaces your tool registry (the quickstart uses a toolset type named agent_toolset_20260401 for the full built-in set).

Everything you learned still applies, because the hosted loop speaks the same protocol. It's simply someone else's code now. That's exactly the trade-off section 14 describes.
3bf2147f3c:
Two practical cautions.

Managed Agents is a beta API. The header (managed-agents-2026-04-01 at the time of writing), endpoint shapes and event names may change between releases. Pin SDK versions, and read the release notes before upgrading.

And sessions are stateful and store outputs. So data-handling reviews should treat a hosted session like any other system of record. Decide retention. Delete sessions and uploaded files through the API when done. Keep secrets out of prompts (chapter 23).
e96df2bb56: If your team's agent will live inside a Spring Boot service, the loop is a few dozen lines with the Anthropic Java SDK. The harness responsibilities map cleanly onto Spring components. Companion example 17 prints this sketch. Builder and accessor names follow the Java SDK's documented style, but check the docs for your SDK version before copying.
c02c69ec89: The saga analogy is most useful at the failure edges. Say an agent run crashes after issuing a credit but before recording the tool result. That's the same problem as a saga participant that committed but whose reply was lost. You need idempotent tools (keyed on the tool_use id) and a persisted log, so the run can resume without repeating side effects. Hosted agents move this problem to Anthropic. Self-hosted agents leave it with you.
193f6ab92f: A harness is ordinary code, and you should test it like ordinary code, without the model. The trick is a fake client that returns scripted responses and validates the requests it receives. Then every protocol bug (a lost id, split results, an unhandled stop reason) fails the test the same way the real API would fail the run. The companion's fake_client.py does this in about a hundred lines. Example 18 then pins down the harness's contract:
0f5a22b60f:
These tests test the harness, not the model. Whether Claude chooses the right tool for a given request is a question for evaluations (chapter 19), run against the real model with graded datasets.

Keeping the two separate is the debugging skill chapter 12 builds on. When a run fails, first ask whether the integration layer (history shape, dispatch, hooks) behaved correctly. These tests answer that deterministically. Only then ask whether the model's output was wrong.
2bbdb8efe4:
For observability, log two kinds of structured record. Log one per model call: session id, turn, model, input and output tokens, cache reads, latency, stop_reason. And log one per tool call: tool_use id, name, arguments after any rewrite, decision and which hook made it, duration, is_error.

With the Agent SDK, a hook with no matcher on PreToolUse and PostToolUse gives you the second record for free. The result message gives you the run-level totals. A run's trace should let a reviewer answer "why did it stop?" without reading the transcript.
ed73f5ab6a: The loop is terminating on text. The response that said "Let me check" had stop_reason: "tool_use". The harness should have run the tool and called again. Raising max_turns, adding "say DONE when finished" to the prompt, or switching models don't address the cause.
a388eb076d: Results must answer every tool_use of the previous assistant turn, in the next user turn. Retrying with backoff treats a protocol error as transient. Disabling parallel tool use hides the bug and costs latency.
fa7d632443: "Every" is a deterministic requirement, and prompts are probabilistic. A stronger prompt or few-shot examples only move the percentage. A Stop hook that formats everything at the end would also work. But it runs later than needed and is coarser. The edit-time hook is the direct answer.
87d52847d9: Long-running, asynchronous, sandboxed work with minimal ops is the documented sweet spot of the hosted harness. A hand-written loop or the Agent SDK would work. But they leave the team to build sandboxing, durable execution and session storage.
